div.head: Ine 28.1
div.ab: Gif he ðonne oðierne ⁊ orige weorðe, þonne bið he wites scyldig.
(⁊) gif he ðonne oþyrne ⁊ orige weorðe, þonne bið he wites scyldig.
Gyf he ðonne oðerna [⁊] orige weorðe, ðonne bið he wites scyldig.
Si repugnet uel aufugiat, reus sit wite.
Gif he ðonne oðierne ⁊ orige weorðe, þonne bið he wites scyldig.
Gif he ðonne oðierne ⁊ orige weorðe, þonne bið he wites scyldig.
Wenn jener [Dieb] jedoch entrinnt und aus den Augen kommt, dann ist jener [Einfänger] Strafgeld schuldig.
But if that [thief] escapes and gets out of sight, then that [captor] is liable to a fine.
If, however, the thief escapes and is lost to sight, then he shall forfeit a fine.
If he, however, runs away and gets out of sight, then he [who captured him] is liable to the fine.
If, however, he escapes and cannot be found, then [the captor] is liable for a fine.

note.seg: ‘sich wehrt’ verschlechtert lq, da orige unverständlich geworden. Leo vermutete vrige ‘bedeckt, versteckt’, Ettmüller orrige ‘ungebunden’, Price urig ‘befleckt’, Thorpe (Glossar) orwige ‘unbefehdet’; ‘offenbar’ übersetzt Schmid. Vgl. anige ‘einäugig’, ahd. urouge ‘aus den Augen; unsichtbar’

lq makes it worse with ‘defends himself’, since orige had become unintelligible. Leo conjectured vrige ‘covered, hidden’, Ettmüller orrige ‘unbound’, Price urig ‘stained’, Thorpe (Glossary) orwige ‘free from feud’; Schmid translates ‘manifest’. Cf. anige ‘one-eyed’, OHG urouge ‘out of sight; invisible’

Vgl. Gl Freilassen von Verbrechern 3. a. Dass der Einfänger auch Busse dem Bestohlenen schulde, meint Schreuer Verbrechenskonk. 45; allein die Eidesschwere in 28, 2 (vgl. 35, 1) berücksichtigt nur den Einersatz neben dem Strafgelde. [Die grössere Strenge in Ine 36 erklärt sich aus absichtlicher Begünstigung.] Das Strafgeld ist vermutlich das, welches der Richter vom Diebe erhalten hätte, käme dieser vor Gericht; es bestimmt zum Gegenstandswerte addiert die Eidesschwere 28, 2. Vielleicht meint auch u. 73 þone gilt ‘jene Schuld’ [des Diebes], nicht wie ich ergänzte [der Unachtsamkeit]. Anders versteht, vielleicht mit Q, Maurer Kr. Übsch. II 53: ‘dann ist er [Dieb nur noch] Strafgeld schuldig [samt Ersatz und Busse, aber nicht, wie der handhafte, Leibesstrafe]’: dies stimmt genau zu 72, harmoniert auch mit 28, 2. Auffallen dabei müsste, dass Ine hier im Ggs. zu 72 erstens das ‘nur’ fortlässt, zweitens vom Wiedereinfang oder von Beklagtwerden des Diebes nichts sagt, vielmehr dessen Verschwinden als dauernd zu fassen durch orige veranlasst

Cf. Gl Freilassen von Verbrechern 3. a. Schreuer Verbrechenskonk. 45 holds that the captor also owes compensation to the man robbed; but the weight of the oath in 28, 2 (cf. 35, 1) takes into account only simple restitution besides the fine. [The greater severity in Ine 36 is explained by deliberate connivance.] The fine is presumably the one the judge would have received from the thief had the latter come before the court; added to the value of the object, it determines the weight of the oath in 28, 2. Perhaps below 73 þone gilt also means ‘that debt’ [of the thief], not, as I supplied, [of negligence]. Maurer Kr. Übsch. II 53 understands it differently, perhaps with Q: ‘then he [the thief is now only] liable to a fine [together with restitution and compensation, but not, like the thief caught in the act, to corporal punishment]’: this agrees exactly with 72 and also harmonises with 28, 2. It would, however, be striking that Ine here, in contrast to 72, first omits the ‘only’, and secondly says nothing of the thief’s recapture or of his being sued, but rather, through orige, gives occasion to take his disappearance as permanent

The reference is presumably to the captor, and not to the thief, for the next paragraph clearly refers to the same person, and allows the possibility of a denial of culpability, which would be hardly feasible in the case of a thief caught in the act (cf. cap. 36. 72. 73).
